title: One body (1 Corinthians 12:12–27)
hookLine: the eye can't say to the hand I don't need you

lines: CLAY HANDS AND FEET IN CORINTH.
cards: Corinth had a healing shrine to the Greek god Asclepius, and people who believed they'd been cured left clay models of the part that got better: a hand, a foot, an ear, an eye. Archaeologists have dug them up there.

Some scholars wonder whether Paul's readers thought of those shelves of separate clay limbs when they heard today's chapter. Because the church in Corinth was falling into pieces. People with showy gifts felt important.
Quiet people felt they didn't count. Paul answers with a body, not a pile of parts.

teach.b: His picture is simple enough for a child. The body has many members, and together they're one body. Then he gives the parts voices.
The foot says: because I am not the hand, I am not of the body. The ear sulks because it isn't an eye. If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be?

teach.h: THE EYE CAN'T SAY: I NEED NOT THY HELP.
teach.b: Then he turns to the ones who feel superior: "And the eye cannot say to the hand: I need not thy help; nor again the head to the feet: I have no need of you."
The members that seem weaker are necessary, and the less honored parts get more care. If one member suffers, all suffer with it; if one is honored, all rejoice.
Then the line it's all been building to: "Now you are the body of Christ, and members of member." The image wasn't new.
The Roman historian Livy tells an old fable of the limbs and the belly, used to persuade the common people to go back to serving the city's rulers.

teach.h: THE WEAKER PARTS GET MORE HONOR.
teach.b: Paul uses the body the other way round, to give the weaker parts more honor.
Catholics read this chapter as one root of a central teaching: the Church is the Mystical Body of Christ, with Christ as the head and the faithful as the members.
Pope Pius the Twelfth wrote a whole encyclical on it in 1943.

teach.h: NOW YOU ARE THE BODY OF CHRIST.
teach.b: It's why Catholics speak of a parish in Lagos and a parish in Ohio as one body, not two clubs, and why the housebound person praying a rosary at home counts as a working member. In this body, nobody is spare.

how: Catholics speak of the Church as the Mystical Body of Christ; at Mass the bidding prayers bring the needs of the sick, the absent and the whole Church before the parish as members of one body.

o: a single leader who does all the work
a group whose members all do the same job
many members, all needed, joined in Christ

games.q: who says what in the body — tap the pairs.
p: because I'm not a hand, I'm not of the body
the body of Christ, members of member

s: Paul says the most visible gifts matter most
he says the members that seem weaker are necessary and get more honor.
in Paul's picture, if one member suffers, all suffer with it
and if one is honored, all rejoice.
for Catholics this passage is only a teamwork metaphor
the Church teaches it is the Mystical Body of Christ; Pius XII wrote an encyclical on it in 1943.

games.q: you have a flashy gift in the Corinthian church. a quiet member asks if they even belong. what does Paul's letter tell you?
o: they belong less, but they can still come.
the parts that seem weaker are necessary.
every gift is the same, so it doesn't matter.
games.why: "the eye cannot say to the hand: I need not thy help." Paul gives the weaker members more honor, not less.

practice: Think of someone whose gift is nothing like yours: a listener if you're a talker, someone who just shows up and fixes things if you're a planner, maybe someone you've quietly thought you could do without.
Picture them, and notice what would fall apart at work, at home or in your parish if they weren't there. If you pray, thank God for them by name.

wordCard.voice: One body. Paul's picture of the Church: many members, every one of them needed, and together the body of Christ. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: body. Paul's word for the Church in 1 Corinthians 12:27, the body of Christ.

carryVoice: Your line: the hand needs the eye. The quiet parts count too. See you tomorrow.
